ExplanationParts.CorpusEarnedOpening: Cutting off the arm is the bodily action attributed to Huike and raised repeatedly as a named ancestral case.
EvidenceBody: In the Chan record it overwhelmingly names the founding episode in which Shenguang, later named Huike, stands in the snow before Bodhidharma, cuts off his left arm, and places it before him. The lamp account has Bodhidharma say, 'you have now cut off your arm before me; your seeking may be accepted,' and then rename him Huike. Later records compress the episode into paired formulas—'standing in the snow and cutting off the arm,' 'cutting off the arm and pacifying the mind,' or 'face the wall for nine years / cut off the arm and pacify the mind'—and repeatedly reopen it as a public question. Huike asks, 'what did the cutting off of the arm accomplish?' and strikes the staff before leaving the seat. Another is asked why one cuts off an arm to seek the Way if this house style is inherent in everyone; he replies, 'there are many mistaken understandings.' Still another says, 'why cut off an arm and seek elsewhere?' The Chan-specific bend is that Huike's bodily act becomes compact lineage and interview language, quoted, challenged, and criticized across later records. These later uses do not authorize this entry to declare the act a required sacrifice or explain its intention beyond what the accounts say.
